# Welcome, game maker! {.unnumbered #welcome}

::: {.book-hero}

[LEARN BY MAKING]{.eyebrow}

[Web Game Coding for Kids]{.hero-title}

*Learn JavaScript by Building 2D and 3D Games*

Build a game. Understand the code. Make it your own.

[18 chapters]{.hero-chip} [Visual explanations]{.hero-chip} [Advanced Study]{.hero-chip}

:::

This book teaches JavaScript in the order a young game designer needs it. Instead of memorizing programming rules first, you will meet a problem inside a game and learn the programming idea that solves it.

::: {.callout-tip .big-idea title="The rule of this book" icon="false"}

Make something move. Make something react. Make something fun. Then study the code that made it happen.

:::

## Your computer toolkit {.unnumbered}

Before you make a game, meet the tools you will use. A **computer** runs programs: sets of instructions that tell it what to do. A web browser is one program. A text editor is another. You are about to write instructions that a browser can follow.

### Files and folders {.unnumbered}

A **file** is one named piece of information saved on a computer. A game picture, a sound, and a page of code can each be files. A **folder** is a container that helps you keep related files together. Think of a folder as a game box and the files inside as its cards, pieces, and rule sheet.

Give each game its own folder. For example, your `my-first-game` folder can hold its HTML page now and later hold pictures, sounds, and more JavaScript files. Keep those files together when you copy or move your game.

### A text editor is for code {.unnumbered}

You write code in a **plain-text editor**. It saves exactly the letters, numbers, spaces, and punctuation that you type. Many editors color code and point out mistakes; that can be helpful, but the colors are not part of the code.

A word processor is great for essays, but it may add special quotation marks, hidden formatting, or page layouts. Those extras can confuse code. Use a plain-text editor for your game files. Ask your teacher which editor is available on your computer.

### File names and extensions {.unnumbered}

The end of a file name after the final dot is its **file extension**. It helps people and programs recognize the file's job.

| File name | Extension | What it usually contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `index.html` | `.html` | The page structure a browser opens. |
| `main.js` | `.js` | JavaScript instructions for the browser. |
| `style.css` | `.css` | Colors, sizes, and other visual choices. |
| `level.json` | `.json` | Organized game data, such as a level layout. |
| `robot.svg` | `.svg` | A picture made from shapes and lines. |

The extension is important. `index.html` and `index.html.txt` are different files: the first is a web page, while the second is usually treated as ordinary text. Some computers hide extensions, so check the full name when you save a file. Do not rename a file just to give it a new extension; save it in the right kind of file from the start.

## Choose your reading path {.unnumbered}

Follow the main explanations and code examples first. Use the diagrams to trace what the program is doing. Then try a challenge and explain your result in your own words.

Chapters 1-12 establish the web and JavaScript foundations. Chapters 13-16 build a complete 2D adventure. Chapters 17-20 introduce Three.js, custom 3D models, and Rapier physics. The later projects take more time and combine earlier ideas; work through them in small experiments.

Purple **Advanced Study** blocks are optional deeper dives into HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and game systems. They start open; you can collapse them while following the main path and return later.

## What you need {.unnumbered}

- A modern web browser such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari.
- A plain-text code editor available on your computer.
- A folder for each website or game containing its files. Chapter 2 begins with separate HTML and CSS files; early JavaScript examples keep their code close to the page so you can focus on the programming ideas.

::: {.callout-tip .setup title="Start with one file" icon="false"}

Create a folder named `my-game-site`. Save your first HTML page as `index.html`, not `index.html.txt`. Open it in your browser. After editing, save the file and refresh the browser. Later, module-based projects need a local development server.

:::

## Meet the browser team {.unnumbered}

Your web browser is the program that turns your game files into a page you can play. Three kinds of code often work together:

| Part | Its job | A game example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **HTML** | Builds the page and names its parts. | A heading, a button, and a canvas. |
| **CSS** | Chooses how those parts look. | A purple button or a large play area. |
| **JavaScript** | Makes the page react and change. | Add a point when the player clicks. |

Think of HTML as the game room, CSS as the paint and decorations, and JavaScript as the rules that make things happen. This book begins with HTML and JavaScript in one file so you can see their connection clearly. CSS will appear when a game needs it.

### What “client-side JavaScript” means {.unnumbered}

The **client** is the player's browser. Client-side JavaScript runs on the same computer, tablet, or Chromebook that displays the game. When a player presses a key, the browser can run your JavaScript right there and update the picture right away.

That is different from code on a **server**—another computer that can store shared scores, accounts, or messages. Our first games do not need a server on the internet. Their rules and scores stay in the browser while the page is open.

## Run a one-file game from your drive {.unnumbered}

For the complete examples in the first chapters, you can run your game directly from your computer's drive.

1. Make a folder called `my-first-game` somewhere you can find again, such as Documents.
2. In a plain-text code editor, save the complete example as `index.html` inside that folder. Check that the name ends in `.html`, not `.html.txt`.
3. Open the folder and double-click `index.html`. Your browser should open it. You may see an address beginning with `file:///`; that means the browser opened a file from your own drive.
4. Return to the editor, make one small change, save, and refresh the browser page. On many computers, refresh is `Ctrl+R` or `Command+R`.

If double-clicking opens an editor instead of a browser, right-click the file and choose **Open with**, then choose your browser. If you cannot see the `.html` ending, ask an adult or teacher to turn on file-name extensions. A file named `index.html.txt` is a text document, not a web page.

## When a local web server helps {.unnumbered}

Some later games use several JavaScript files, images, level-data files, or 3D models. A **web server** is a small program that hands files to a browser when the browser asks for them. It is like a careful librarian: the browser asks for a particular file, and the server gives back that file.

For a one-file beginner game, `file:///` is enough. For a project that uses JavaScript `import`, JSON data, or files loaded by the game, start a **local web server** instead. A local server runs only on your own computer and gives the page an address such as `http://127.0.0.1:8000/`. Modern browsers use extra safety rules for those multi-file requests, so opening the HTML by double-clicking may not work.

`127.0.0.1` means “this same computer.” Starting this book's local server does not put your game on the internet or let classmates visit it. The Game Lab instructions in [Appendix E](#sec-game-lab) show exactly how to start it.

## Read examples carefully {.unnumbered}

A **complete example** includes the setup for that small project. A **code fragment** illustrates one part of a game and relies on the variables or functions discussed nearby. Do not paste every fragment into one file without checking where it belongs: some examples replace earlier versions.

Chapters 9-11 use Pong, Breakout, and Snake to explain larger game-building patterns. Their snippets are building blocks rather than full finished games. Chapters 13-20 add complete companion projects in the Game Lab. Their chapter snippets explain selected parts; the linked project folders contain the complete runnable source.

## A safe learning habit {.unnumbered}

When a program does not work, do not immediately replace it with someone else's code. Read the browser console, compare one small section at a time, and explain what you expected to happen. Debugging is part of programming, not evidence that you failed.

## Open the Game Lab {.unnumbered}

The companion Game Lab contains six complete projects, including two experimental labs, two collectible adventures, a 3D exploration game, and a model-customization workshop. Keep the project folders together so their shared code and assets can be found.

::: {.callout-tip .setup title="Run the later projects" icon="false"}
From the extracted textbook folder, run `node scripts/serve.mjs`. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/games/` in your browser. This local server needs Node.js but no package installation. Use the [Game Lab guide](#sec-game-lab) for controls, file locations, and troubleshooting.

The 2D projects use local files only. The 3D projects initially download pinned Three.js and Rapier modules from a CDN, so they need an internet connection and a browser with WebGL2. An optional dependency-download script supports later offline use.

# Meet Your Computer, Browser, and the Web {#sec-ch01}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[WEB 01 | Your first web workspace]{.game-title}

[Personal computer]{.skill-chip} [Browser]{.skill-chip} [Files]{.skill-chip} [Servers]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- name the jobs of your computer, browser, files, and web servers
- organize a small website in its own folder
- explain the difference between a local file and a web address
- predict where HTML, CSS, and JavaScript will do their work

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

Your browser is a program on **your** computer. It can open files saved on that computer or ask a server on the internet for files. In both cases, the browser assembles the page that you see.

:::

![A project folder on a personal computer can send a local file directly to its browser. The browser can also request files from a web server through the internet, then receive the response and show the page.](../figures/chapter_01/client-browser-server.svg){#fig-ch01-client-server fig-alt="A diagram shows a project folder and a browser client inside a personal computer. The browser opens local files from the folder or sends a request through the internet to a web server, which returns page files." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** The folder, browser, and client are all on the same personal computer. The server is only involved when the browser uses an internet address. In both routes, the browser is the program that displays the page.

## Your personal computer is your first web workshop

A **personal computer** is the device in front of you: perhaps a laptop, desktop, or Chromebook. It stores files and runs programs. Two programs matter especially in this book:

- A **text editor** lets you write and save code as plain text.
- A **web browser**—such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari—reads web files and shows a page.

When your browser is doing the work on your device, your device is called the **client**. “Client” does not mean a different kind of computer. It means the computer that asks for a page and uses it.

For the first pages in this book, the client is all you need. You will save a file, open it in your browser, edit it, save again, and refresh the page to see the change.

## Keep each website in its own folder

A website is a group of related files. Make one folder for one project so its files stay together. For the next chapter, create a folder named `my-game-site` with these two files inside it:

```
my-game-site/
  index.html
  styles.css
```

`index.html` will describe the page. `styles.css` will describe its colors, spacing, and layout. The endings after the dots are part of the file names:

- `.html` means an HTML page.
- `.css` means a CSS style sheet.
- `.js` will later mean a JavaScript program.

Be careful to save plain-text files with the right ending. A file named `index.html.txt` is a text document, not a web page. If you cannot see file endings, ask a teacher or an adult to help turn them on.

## The browser turns files into a page

When you open `index.html`, the browser reads the HTML instructions and creates the page. If the HTML links to `styles.css`, the browser reads that file too. It uses CSS to decide how the same page should look.

Think of the jobs this way:

| Tool or file | Main job | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTML | structure and meaning | a heading, a paragraph, a button |
| CSS | appearance and layout | a blue button, a roomy card, a centered title |
| JavaScript | behavior that changes | what happens after a player clicks |

HTML and CSS can make a useful, polished **static website**. “Static” means that the page does not yet run its own rules or change itself. A button can look like a game button before it has JavaScript to react to a click.

## Try two local browser examples

This book project now includes two tiny example pages in `workspace/chapter1/`. Open `index.html` from that folder, then choose an example. They use only files saved on the computer, so you do not need an internet connection or a server.

The first page shows how many HTML elements can work together. It has a page title, navigation links, headings, paragraphs, a picture, an ordered list, and a table. CSS gives the elements their colors, spacing, and card-like layout.

![A Chrome rendering of a local HTML example page. The page has a Pixel Planet header, navigation links, a large heading, a paragraph, a rocket image, an ordered mission list, and a table that names the jobs of several HTML elements.](../figures/chapter_01/html-elements-browser.png){#fig-ch01-html-elements fig-alt="A local browser page titled Welcome, space explorer. It shows a header with links, a rocket image, an ordered list, and a table that explains heading, paragraph, and link elements." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** Every visible piece started as an HTML element. HTML explains what each piece is; the separate CSS file decides how the pieces are arranged and styled.

## Local files and web addresses

You can open a saved file directly from your computer. Its address often begins with `file:///`. For example, it might look similar to this:

```
file:///Users/your-name/Documents/my-game-site/index.html
```

This address means, “Browser, open this file from this computer.” It does not put your page on the internet.

An internet address usually begins with `https://`, such as `https://example.com`. That tells the browser to contact a **server**. A server is a computer program that keeps web files ready and sends a requested file back to a browser.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="A browser request, step by step" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

When you visit an internet address, the browser first finds the server for that address. Then it sends a **request**, such as “Please send the home page.” The server sends a **response**, such as the HTML file. The browser may make more requests for the page's CSS, pictures, fonts, or JavaScript.

The server supplies files; the browser on the client turns them into the page. A later game might ask a server for an image or level file, but its drawing and player controls can still run in the browser.

:::

## Two kinds of servers you will meet

A public server is connected to the internet so many people can visit a website. We will not publish anything in this book.

A **local server** runs only on your own computer. It gives files an address such as `http://127.0.0.1:8000/`. `127.0.0.1` means “this same computer.” Later, when games use several JavaScript files, data files, or 3D models, a local server helps the browser load them safely. Starting one does not make your project public.

For now, opening `index.html` directly is enough. Learn the page's structure and style first; the next chapter does exactly that.

## Get ready for input and JavaScript

Web pages have **input elements** such as text boxes, checkboxes, menus, and buttons. In the next chapter, you will place them on a static site and label them clearly. They will be real browser controls, but they will not yet make a game remember a choice or react to a click.

Here is the second local browser example. It puts several input elements on one player-card page: text, email, number, and date fields; a menu; a color picker; a slider; radio buttons; a checkbox; a text area; and a button.

![A Chrome rendering of a local player-card form. It contains fields for nickname, email, number, date, a menu, color picker, range slider, radio buttons, checkbox, text area, and a button that says JavaScript comes next.](../figures/chapter_01/input-elements-browser.png){#fig-ch01-input-elements fig-alt="A browser page titled Design your player card with labeled text, email, number, date, select, color, range, radio, checkbox, text area, and button controls." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** The controls are already real browser elements. A person can type and choose, but the page has no JavaScript yet to save the answers, calculate with them, or react to the button.

That is intentional. First learn what HTML puts on a page and what CSS changes about its appearance. Then, in Chapter 3, JavaScript will find those elements and give them behavior.

# Build a Static Website with HTML and CSS {#sec-ch02}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[WEB 02 | Game Maker HQ]{.game-title}

[HTML]{.skill-chip} [CSS]{.skill-chip} [Forms]{.skill-chip} [Page structure]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- make an HTML page and connect a CSS file to it
- use headings, sections, lists, and classes to give a page structure
- use basic CSS rules, selectors, and declarations
- change font family, size, weight, and style to give a site its voice
- style a local image with size, borders, rounded corners, and a shadow
- add labeled text, menu, checkbox, and button input elements

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

HTML says what belongs on a page. CSS says how it should look. Together they make a static website—the visual stage that JavaScript will make interactive in the next chapter.

:::

## Make the project folder

Create the folder from Chapter 1 and open it in your text editor:

```
my-game-site/
  index.html
  styles.css
  gem.svg
```

Keep the files in the same folder. The HTML file will use a `<link>` element to tell the browser where to find the CSS file. Copy [gem.svg](../games/assets/2d/gem.svg) from this textbook into your new folder so the page can show a local image.

## Build the page with HTML

Save this complete example as `index.html`. HTML tags use angle brackets. Most tags have an opening tag and a matching closing tag; the content goes between them.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `index.html`]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Game Maker HQ</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <main class="card">
    <p class="eyebrow">MY STATIC WEBSITE</p>
    <h1>Game Maker HQ</h1>
    <p class="intro">Plan the next game you want to build.</p>

    <section class="game-preview">
      <img class="game-art" src="gem.svg"
           alt="A shiny purple gem for a game treasure.">
      <div>
        <h2>Gem Quest</h2>
        <p>Collect three gems, then open the portal.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section>
      <h2>Today's missions</h2>
      <ul>
        <li>Sketch one game character.</li>
        <li>Choose a goal for the player.</li>
        <li>Invent a fair challenge.</li>
      </ul>
    </section>

    <section>
      <h2>Player card</h2>
      <form>
        <label for="player-name">Your game-maker name</label>
        <input id="player-name" name="player-name" type="text"
               placeholder="Type a nickname">

        <label for="game-type">Game type</label>
        <select id="game-type" name="game-type">
          <option>Adventure</option>
          <option>Puzzle</option>
          <option>Sports</option>
        </select>

        <label class="check-row" for="sound-on">
          <input id="sound-on" name="sound-on" type="checkbox">
          I want sound effects in my game.
        </label>

        <button type="button">My game will use this later</button>
      </form>
    </section>

    <p class="hint">This is a static site: the controls are ready, but JavaScript has not given them behavior yet.</p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `index.html` in a browser. If you edit it, save the file and refresh the browser tab. The page will have structure, but it will look plain until you add the CSS. A ready-to-run copy of these files is in `workspace/chapter2/`; open `plain.html` there to see the same page with its stylesheet link removed.

![The Game Maker HQ page in Chrome before its CSS file is linked. The headings, mission list, gem image, and player form appear in the browser's default style.](../figures/chapter_02/game-maker-hq-plain.png){#fig-ch02-plain-page fig-alt="A plain white browser page shows Game Maker HQ, a small gem, three missions, and a player form with default browser controls." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** The content is already in a useful order: heading, game preview, missions, then player card. The gem loads because its `<img>` path points to a real local file. Without the stylesheet link, the browser supplies its default fonts, spacing, and control layout.

### Read the important HTML pieces {.unnumbered}

- `<head>` holds information *about* the page. The browser-tab title and the CSS link belong there.
- `<body>` holds the parts people see and use.
- `<main>` groups the main content. Its `class="card"` gives CSS a useful name for this group.
- `<h1>` and `<h2>` are headings. `<p>` is a paragraph. `<ul>` and `<li>` make a list.
- `<section>` groups a related part of the page.
- `<img>` puts the local `gem.svg` picture on the page. Its `alt` text describes the picture for people who cannot see it.

## CSS basics: rules change how HTML looks

CSS is a list of rules. A rule starts with a **selector**—the HTML element or class that you want to style. Inside the braces, each **declaration** has a property, a colon, a value, and a semicolon.

```css
selector {
  property: value;
}
```

Read this rule aloud as: “For every element with the class `game-art`, make the border rounded.”

```css
.game-art {
  border-radius: 24px;
}
```

The dot is important. `.game-art` means “find `class="game-art"` in the HTML.” An element selector has no dot: `h1` styles every level-one heading and `img` styles every image. You can write more than one declaration inside the same braces.

| Selector | What it selects | Example use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `body` | the whole visible page | choose a default font and text color |
| `h1` | every main heading | make the title large and bold |
| `.intro` | elements with `class="intro"` | make the introduction italic |
| `.game-art` | the gem image with that class | set the image's frame and size |

## Style fonts and images with CSS

Save this in a second file named `styles.css`.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `styles.css`]{.code-label}

```css
:root {
  --ink: #17243b;
  --paper: #f7f4ff;
  --purple: #6d3df5;
  --yellow: #ffe48a;
}

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  min-height: 100vh;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #c9efff, var(--paper));
  color: var(--ink);
  font-family: "Trebuchet MS", Verdana, sans-serif;
  font-size: 1rem;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

.card {
  width: min(92%, 620px);
  margin: 32px;
  padding: 32px;
  border: 4px solid var(--ink);
  border-radius: 24px;
  background: white;
  box-shadow: 10px 10px 0 var(--yellow);
}

.eyebrow {
  margin: 0;
  color: var(--purple);
  font-family: Verdana, sans-serif;
  font-size: 0.8rem;
  font-weight: 700;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
}

h1 {
  margin: 8px 0;
  color: var(--purple);
  font-family: Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
  font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 7vw, 3.5rem);
  font-weight: 800;
  line-height: 1.1;
}

.intro {
  color: #4c3f74;
  font-size: 1.15rem;
  font-style: italic;
}

.hint {
  font-size: 0.9rem;
}

.game-preview {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 22px;
  margin-top: 28px;
  padding: 18px;
  border: 2px solid #b7aee5;
  border-radius: 20px;
  background: #f2edff;
}

.game-preview h2 {
  margin: 0;
  font-family: Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
}

.game-preview p {
  margin: 4px 0 0;
}

.game-art {
  width: 140px;
  height: 140px;
  padding: 14px;
  border: 4px solid var(--purple);
  border-radius: 24px;
  background: white;
  box-shadow: 7px 7px 0 var(--yellow);
  object-fit: contain;
}

section {
  margin-top: 28px;
  padding-top: 8px;
  border-top: 2px dashed #b7aee5;
}

form {
  display: grid;
  gap: 10px;
}

input,
select,
button {
  min-height: 44px;
  padding: 10px 12px;
  border: 2px solid var(--ink);
  border-radius: 10px;
  font: inherit;
}

.check-row {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 8px;
}

.check-row input {
  min-height: auto;
}

button {
  margin-top: 8px;
  background: var(--purple);
  color: white;
  cursor: pointer;
  font-weight: 800;
}

button:hover {
  background: #4d24c8;
}

input:focus-visible,
select:focus-visible,
button:focus-visible {
  outline: 4px solid var(--yellow);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

@media (max-width: 520px) {
  .game-preview {
    align-items: flex-start;
    flex-direction: column;
  }
}
```

Save `styles.css` beside `index.html`, then refresh the page. Compare this browser result with the plain version above. The HTML content is the same; the linked CSS file changes its appearance.

![The Game Maker HQ page in Chrome after the linked CSS file is loaded. A centered white card contains a large purple title, framed gem preview, spaced missions, and stacked form controls.](../figures/chapter_02/game-maker-hq-styled.png){#fig-ch02-styled-page fig-alt="A styled Game Maker HQ page has a pale blue background, white card, purple title, framed gem, mission list, and full-width player form controls." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** `.card` makes the white panel, `.game-preview` arranges the gem and its text, and `.game-art` adds the gem's rounded frame and shadow. The `form` rule stacks the labeled controls. Try changing one CSS value, saving, and refreshing to see which part of this picture changes.

### Give the site a readable voice {.unnumbered}

```css
body {
  font-family: "Trebuchet MS", Verdana, sans-serif;
}

h1 {
  font-family: Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
  font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 7vw, 3.5rem);
  font-weight: 800;
}

.intro {
  font-style: italic;
}
```

`font-family` chooses the lettering style. The comma-separated names are a **font stack**: the browser tries the first font and then tries the next one if needed. The last name, such as `sans-serif` or `serif`, is a broad backup family, so the page still has a sensible look on another computer.

`font-size` changes how large the letters appear. `font-weight` changes how thick they look: `400` is similar to normal text, while `700` is similar to bold. `font-style: italic` adds a slant for emphasis. Use the right HTML tag first—an `<h1>` should still be the main heading even if you later change its size with CSS.

### Frame an image with CSS {.unnumbered}

```css
.game-art {
  width: 140px;
  padding: 14px;
  border: 4px solid var(--purple);
  border-radius: 24px;
  box-shadow: 7px 7px 0 var(--yellow);
}
```

`width` keeps the image at a friendly size. `padding` adds breathing room inside its frame. `border` draws the edge, `border-radius` rounds the corners, and `box-shadow` makes the gem look as if it is resting above the card. Try changing `border-radius` to `50%`; the square frame becomes a circle.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Practice CSS one property at a time" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Change one value, save the CSS file, and refresh the browser. That small experiment tells you exactly which property made the difference. Helpful next references are the [W3Schools CSS tutorial](https://www.w3schools.com/css/), [CSS Fonts](https://www.w3schools.com/css/css_font.asp), and [CSS Styling Images](https://www.w3schools.com/css/css3_images.asp).

:::

## Prepare the inputs for JavaScript

The text box, menu, checkbox, and button are all **input elements**: parts of a page a person can use. Their labels make the controls easier to understand and help assistive technology describe them.

Look closely at this pair:

```html
<label for="player-name">Your game-maker name</label>
<input id="player-name" name="player-name" type="text">
```

The label's `for="player-name"` matches the input's `id="player-name"`. That connection means clicking the words “Your game-maker name” focuses the correct text box. The `id` will also let JavaScript find this exact element later.

The button uses `type="button"`. It looks and feels like a button, but it has no task yet. It will not submit the form or save the choices. JavaScript needs to listen for a click, read the inputs, and decide what to do.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Static does not mean unfinished" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Static pages are excellent for information, art portfolios, instructions, and game-planning pages. HTML gives them a sensible order; CSS makes them readable and expressive. JavaScript is only needed when the page must respond, calculate, remember, fetch data, or change while it is open.

The browser may remember what you typed for a moment, but this example has no code to save a player name. Refreshing or reopening the page can clear it. Code that remembers choices comes later.

:::

# Make the Page React {#sec-ch03}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 03 | Click the Monster]{.game-title}

[Events]{.skill-chip} [Functions]{.skill-chip} [HTML]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- connect JavaScript to a button
- write and call a function
- respond to a click event

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

A game begins when the player does something and the program reacts. In the browser, those actions are called events.

:::

## Your first game screen

We will start with one HTML file. The button is our monster. When the player clicks it, JavaScript runs a function.

![Event flow: a player action becomes a JavaScript response.](../figures/chapter_01/event-flow.png){#fig-ch03 fig-alt="A player clicks the monster button, the browser detects a click event, and JavaScript calls hitMonster." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** Follow the arrows from left to right. The player creates the event; the browser notices it; the registered function supplies the response. Registering a listener does not run the function immediately.

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <h1>Click the Monster!</h1>
  <button id="monster">👾 Monster</button>
  <script>
    // JavaScript goes here
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

## Give HTML and JavaScript their jobs

Look at the example as two teammates sharing one file. **HTML** tells the browser what belongs on the page. **Client-side JavaScript** is the code inside `<script>`; the browser runs it on the player's device.

```html
<h1>Click the Monster!</h1>       <!-- a page heading -->
<button id="monster">👾 Monster</button> <!-- a clickable button -->
<script>
  // JavaScript instructions go here.
</script>
```

The `<h1>` and `<button>` tags create things the player can see. The `id="monster"` gives the button a unique nickname that JavaScript can use later. The `<script>` tags tell the browser, “the words inside are JavaScript.”

When the player clicks, the browser runs this JavaScript right in that browser. That is why it is called **client-side**: the player's device is the client. Nothing in this tiny game needs to be sent to a website. Your score or message lasts while the page is open; reloading the page starts its memory over.

## A function is an action you can name

A function groups instructions. Think of a function as a named card in a game's rule box: when someone uses its name, the instructions on the card happen. The function below is named `hitMonster`. Nothing inside it runs yet; we are only making the card and giving it a name.

```javascript
function hitMonster() {
  alert("You hit the monster!");
}
```

## Connect the click to the function

Now JavaScript needs to find the button and tell it what to do. Long code names can look scary, so we will translate them one piece at a time.

```javascript
const monster = document.getElementById("monster");
monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
```

![JavaScript asks the current page for the button named monster, tells it to listen for a click, and runs hitMonster when the player clicks.](../figures/chapter_01/find-listen-react.svg){#fig-ch03-find-listen fig-alt="A diagram shows a browser page with a Monster button whose ID is monster. JavaScript asks document.getElementById for monster, stores the returned button in monster, adds a click listener, and runs hitMonster when the player clicks." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** The two uses of `monster` are connected, but they are not quite the same thing. In HTML, `id="monster"` is the button's nickname. In JavaScript, `const monster` is a box that holds the button after JavaScript finds it.

### First line: find the button {.unnumbered}

```javascript
const monster = document.getElementById("monster");
```

Read this as: **“Ask this page for the element whose ID is `monster`, then keep it in a box named `monster`.”**

- `document` does **not** mean a school report or a file in your folder. In browser JavaScript, it means the web page that is open right now.
- `get` means “find and give me.”
- An **element** is one piece of a web page, such as a button, a heading, or a paragraph.
- `ById` means “use its unique ID nickname.” We gave the button that nickname in HTML: `<button id="monster">`.
- The quoted `"monster"` is the information we give to `getElementById()`. Quotes mean it is text. JavaScript checks the page for an ID spelled exactly `monster`—same letters, same lowercase `m`.
- `const monster =` makes a named box called `monster` and saves the found button in it. This JavaScript name could be `monsterButton` instead, but using the same nickname makes the first example easier to follow.

The dots are like saying “go to the next helper.” `document.getElementById` means “use the page's helper named `getElementById`.” The parentheses hold the information we give that helper.

### Second line: listen for a click {.unnumbered}

```javascript
monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
```

An **event** is something that happens, such as a click, a key press, or moving a mouse. A **listener** is a helper that waits and notices one kind of event. So `addEventListener` means: **“attach a listener that waits for an event.”**

This line says: **“Tell the button in the `monster` box to wait for a click. When a click happens, use the action named `hitMonster`.”**

- `"click"` tells the listener which event to watch for. It is text, so it needs quotes.
- The comma separates two pieces of information: first the event to watch for, then the action to use.
- `hitMonster` has no parentheses here because we are handing the browser the action card for later. Writing `hitMonster()` would run the action immediately, before the player clicks.

The listener keeps waiting while the game is open. It does not make the button click by itself.

## Build the complete game

Put the pieces together. Type the code yourself if you can; typing helps your brain notice punctuation, spelling, and structure.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <h1>Click the Monster!</h1>
  <button id="monster">👾 Monster</button>
  <p id="message">Can you catch it?</p>

  <script>
    const monster = document.getElementById("monster");
    const message = document.getElementById("message");

    function hitMonster() {
      message.textContent = "Great hit!";
    }

    monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

Open the runnable copy at `workspace/chapter3/monster.html`, or save the complete example above as `index.html` and open it in a browser. Before a click, the paragraph asks the player to catch the monster.

![Click the Monster in Chrome before the button is clicked. The message asks, Can you catch it?](../figures/chapter_03/monster-before-click.png){#fig-ch03-monster-before fig-alt="The Click the Monster page shows a Monster button and the message Can you catch it?" width="100%"}

![Click the Monster in Chrome after the button is clicked. The message changes to Great hit!](../figures/chapter_03/monster-after-click.png){#fig-ch03-monster-after fig-alt="The same Click the Monster page shows the unchanged button and the new message Great hit!" width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** The heading and button stay in place. The click listener runs `hitMonster()`, and `message.textContent` replaces only the paragraph's text. The `monster-after-click.html` companion makes that click automatically for the second screenshot.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Second example | Click a picture" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL IMAGE UPGRADE]{.study-badge}

Buttons are useful, but a game can also react when the player clicks a picture. Copy [gem.svg](../games/assets/2d/gem.svg) from this textbook into your `my-first-game` folder. Keep the name `gem.svg`. The image and your `index.html` file must be in the same folder.

~~~html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <h1>Click the Gem!</h1>
  <img id="gem" src="gem.svg"
       alt="A purple gem. Click it to collect it." width="96">
  <p id="message">The gem is waiting.</p>

  <script>
    const gem = document.getElementById("gem");
    const message = document.getElementById("message");

    function collectGem() {
      message.textContent = "You collected the gem!";
    }

    gem.addEventListener("click", collectGem);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
~~~

Open `workspace/chapter3/gem.html` to try this picture version. The gem image appears before you click it; the paragraph starts with “The gem is waiting.”

![Click the Gem in Chrome before the gem is clicked. The message says The gem is waiting.](../figures/chapter_03/gem-before-click.png){#fig-ch03-gem-before fig-alt="The Click the Gem page shows a purple gem image above the message The gem is waiting." width="100%"}

![Click the Gem in Chrome after the gem is clicked. The message changes to You collected the gem!](../figures/chapter_03/gem-after-click.png){#fig-ch03-gem-after fig-alt="The same Click the Gem page shows the purple gem and the new message You collected the gem!" width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** The image itself receives the click. `getElementById("gem")` finds it, and its listener runs `collectGem()`. Only the message changes. `workspace/chapter3/gem-after-click.html` makes the click automatically for the second screenshot.

The `<img>` tag puts a picture on the page. Its `src="gem.svg"` tells the browser which picture file to load. Its `alt` text describes the picture for players who cannot see it. We use `id="gem"` and `getElementById("gem")` for the same reason we used `monster` before: JavaScript needs a unique nickname for the picture it should listen to.

This is still a one-file game plus one local picture file. You can open `index.html` directly from your drive; you do not need a local server yet.

:::

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | HTML elements and the DOM" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

HTML gives the browser a structure. JavaScript does not usually change the HTML file itself while the game is running; it changes the browser’s in-memory page map called the **DOM**. `getElementById()` returns one item from that map, and `addEventListener()` attaches behavior without mixing JavaScript directly into the HTML tag.

```javascript
const monster = document.getElementById('monster');
monster.addEventListener('click', hitMonster);
```

**HTML and JavaScript have different jobs.** In `<button id="monster">Monster</button>`, `button` identifies the kind of element, `id` gives it a unique name on this page, and the text between the tags becomes its label. The JavaScript lookup must match that ID exactly.

**Why is the script at the bottom?** The browser reaches the button before the script tries to find it. Keep that order. If the lookup finds nothing, it returns `null`.

**Function name or function call?** Pass `hitMonster` to the listener so the browser can call it later. Writing `hitMonster()` calls it immediately.

:::

# Teach the Game to Remember {#sec-ch04}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 04 | Treasure Clicker]{.game-title}

[Variables]{.skill-chip} [Strings]{.skill-chip} [DOM]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- create variables with let and `const`
- change a variable
- show a value on the page

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

A score is memory. The game needs a place to store a number and change it after each successful action.

:::

## Variables are labeled storage

Use let when a value will change. Use `const` when the variable should keep referring to the same thing.

![A variable is a named place for a value that can change.](../figures/chapter_02/variable-memory.png){#fig-ch04 fig-alt="The variable score refers to 7. Executing score equals score plus 1 replaces 7 with 8." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** First read the old value, 7. Add 1 to get 8. Finally, assign 8 back to `score`. The label stays the same while the value changes.

```javascript
let score = 0;
const treasure = document.getElementById("treasure");
```

## Updating the score

The assignment operator = stores a new value. `score = score + 1` means: take the old score, add one, and store the result back into score.

```javascript
function collectTreasure() {
  score = score + 1;
  scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;
}
```

## Strings and numbers

Text inside quotes is a string. A score such as 7 is a number. JavaScript can join text and a number with + when text is involved.

```javascript
let playerName = "Maya";
let score = 7;
message.textContent = playerName + " has " + score + " gems!";
```

## Build the complete game

Put the pieces together. Type the code yourself if you can; typing helps your brain notice punctuation, spelling, and structure.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <h1>Treasure Clicker</h1>
  <button id="treasure">💎 Collect treasure</button>
  <p id="score">Score: 0</p>

  <script>
    let score = 0;
    const treasure = document.getElementById("treasure");
    const scoreText = document.getElementById("score");

    function collectTreasure() {
      score = score + 1;
      scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;
    }

    treasure.addEventListener("click", collectTreasure);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `workspace/chapter4-treasure/button.html` to run the complete example, or save the code above as `index.html`. The score starts at zero. The `button-three-clicks.html` companion clicks the button three times automatically for the second screenshot.

![Treasure Clicker in Chrome before the button is clicked. Its score is zero.](../figures/chapter_04/treasure-button-start.png){#fig-ch04-button-start fig-alt="The Treasure Clicker page shows a Collect treasure button and Score: 0." width="100%"}

![Treasure Clicker in Chrome after three button clicks. Its score is three.](../figures/chapter_04/treasure-button-three-clicks.png){#fig-ch04-button-three fig-alt="The same Treasure Clicker page shows Score: 3 after three button clicks." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** The click listener calls `collectTreasure()` each time. `score = score + 1` remembers the new number; `scoreText.textContent` displays it. The heading and button do not change. Refresh to start again at zero.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Second example | Collect a picture" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL IMAGE UPGRADE]{.study-badge}

Turn the treasure button into a picture. First, copy [gem.svg](../games/assets/2d/gem.svg) into the same folder as your `index.html` file. The JavaScript works almost the same way: an image is also a page element, so it can listen for clicks.

~~~html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <h1>Gem Collector</h1>
  <img id="treasure" src="gem.svg"
       alt="A purple gem. Click it to collect it." width="96">
  <p id="score">Score: 0</p>

  <script>
    let score = 0;
    const treasure = document.getElementById("treasure");
    const scoreText = document.getElementById("score");

    function collectTreasure() {
      score = score + 1;
      scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;
    }

    treasure.addEventListener("click", collectTreasure);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
~~~

Open `workspace/chapter4-treasure/gem.html` to try this version. Its score also begins at zero, and the gem itself is the thing to click. The `gem-three-clicks.html` companion clicks it three times automatically for the second screenshot.

![Gem Collector in Chrome before the gem is clicked. Its score is zero.](../figures/chapter_04/treasure-gem-start.png){#fig-ch04-gem-start fig-alt="The Gem Collector page shows a purple gem above Score: 0." width="100%"}

![Gem Collector in Chrome after three clicks on the gem. Its score is three.](../figures/chapter_04/treasure-gem-three-clicks.png){#fig-ch04-gem-three fig-alt="The same Gem Collector page shows Score: 3 after three gem clicks." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** Here `treasure` refers to the `<img>` element. Its click listener runs the same `collectTreasure()` function as the button version, so the score update works without changing the game rule.

The name `treasure` is only a helpful label. In this example, it refers to a gem picture instead of a button. Try clicking the gem several times. Each click is an event, so the same `collectTreasure` function can add another point.

:::

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | let, const, scope, and types" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Use `const` when a name should not be reassigned and let when the stored value needs to change. JavaScript is dynamically typed: a variable is not permanently locked to one type. For beginning games, keep each variable consistent—scores stay numbers, names stay strings, and element references stay DOM objects.

```javascript
let score = 0;
const scoreLabel = document.getElementById('score');
scoreLabel.textContent = score;
```

**A constant is not a frozen object.** `const scoreLabel` keeps the same element reference, but `scoreLabel.textContent` can still change. What cannot change is which element the name refers to.

**Scope means where a name is available.** A `let` or `const` declared inside block braces is available within that block, not everywhere. Our score lives outside the click function so repeated clicks share it.

**Predict before running:** How do `7 + 1` and `"7" + 1` differ? The first adds numbers; the second joins text.

:::

# Let the Game Make Decisions {#sec-ch05}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 05 | Secret Number]{.game-title}

[Input]{.skill-chip} [Decisions]{.skill-chip} [Comparisons]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- read a player value
- compare values
- use if, `else if`, and `else`

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

Games constantly ask questions: Did the player touch the enemy? Is the timer finished? Is this guess too high? An if statement lets code choose what happens next.

:::

## Read input

The value property reads what a player typed. `Number(...)` converts text such as "7" into the number 7.

![Decision flow: conditions choose which code path runs.](../figures/chapter_03/decision-flow.png){#fig-ch05 fig-alt="A decision branches on whether a guess equals the secret. Yes gives success; no asks for another clue." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** A condition chooses one path. In our game, the first check is equality. Only when it is false do the later checks decide between too low and too high.

```javascript
const guessBox = document.getElementById("guess");
const guess = Number(guessBox.value);
```

## Ask a yes/no question

A comparison produces `true` or `false`. `===` asks whether two values are equal in both value and type.

```javascript
if (guess === secret) {
  message.textContent = "You found it!";
}
```

## More than two choices

`else if` lets the program check another condition when the first one was `false`.

```javascript
if (guess === secret) {
  message.textContent = "Correct!";
} else if (guess < secret) {
  message.textContent = "Too low!";
} else {
  message.textContent = "Too high!";
}
```

## Build the complete game

Put the pieces together. Type the code yourself if you can; typing helps your brain notice punctuation, spelling, and structure.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <h1>Secret Number</h1>
  <input id="guess" type="number" min="1" max="10">
  <button id="check">Check</button>
  <p id="message">Guess a number from 1 to 10.</p>

  <script>
    const secret = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) + 1;
    const guessBox = document.getElementById("guess");
    const message = document.getElementById("message");

    document.getElementById("check").addEventListener("click", function () {
      const guess = Number(guessBox.value);
      if (guess === secret) {
        message.textContent = "Correct!";
      } else if (guess < secret) {
        message.textContent = "Too low!";
      } else {
        message.textContent = "Too high!";
      }
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `workspace/chapter5-secret-number/number.html` to try this example, or save the code above as `index.html`. The normal game chooses a new secret from 1 to 10 on each load. For these browser screenshots, the companion demonstration pages fix the secret at 6 and make one guess automatically.

![Secret Number in Chrome after guessing 3 when the secret is 6. The clue is Too low!](../figures/chapter_05/number-too-low.png){#fig-ch05-number-low fig-alt="The Secret Number page has 3 in the input and shows Too low! below the Check button." width="100%"}

![Secret Number in Chrome after guessing 9 when the secret is 6. The clue is Too high!](../figures/chapter_05/number-too-high.png){#fig-ch05-number-high fig-alt="The Secret Number page has 9 in the input and shows Too high! below the Check button." width="100%"}

![Secret Number in Chrome after guessing 6 when the secret is 6. The clue is Correct!](../figures/chapter_05/number-correct.png){#fig-ch05-number-correct fig-alt="The Secret Number page has 6 in the input and shows Correct! below the Check button." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** Each click converts the input text to a number. For 3, the first comparison is false and `guess < secret` is true. For 9, both comparisons are false, so `else` runs. For 6, `guess === secret` is true, so the game displays “Correct!” and skips the other branches.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Second example | Let a picture give feedback" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL IMAGE UPGRADE]{.study-badge}

Games can use pictures as clues, not only words. Copy [gem.svg](../games/assets/2d/gem.svg) and [bug.svg](../games/assets/2d/bug.svg) into the same folder as `index.html`. In this version, a bug picture means “keep guessing,” and a gem picture appears when the player finds the secret number.

~~~html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <h1>Secret Number</h1>
  <input id="guess" type="number" min="1" max="10">
  <button id="check">Check</button>
  <p id="message">Guess a number from 1 to 10.</p>
  <img id="feedback" src="bug.svg"
       alt="A bug means you have not found the secret yet." width="96">

  <script>
    const secret = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) + 1;
    const guessBox = document.getElementById("guess");
    const message = document.getElementById("message");
    const feedback = document.getElementById("feedback");

    document.getElementById("check").addEventListener("click", function () {
      const guess = Number(guessBox.value);

      if (guess === secret) {
        message.textContent = "Correct!";
        feedback.src = "gem.svg";
        feedback.alt = "A gem means you found the secret number.";
      } else if (guess < secret) {
        message.textContent = "Too low!";
        feedback.src = "bug.svg";
        feedback.alt = "A bug means you should keep guessing.";
      } else {
        message.textContent = "Too high!";
        feedback.src = "bug.svg";
        feedback.alt = "A bug means you should keep guessing.";
      }
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>
~~~

Open `workspace/chapter5-secret-number/picture.html` to run this version. The companion demonstration pages again use 6 as the secret so the two browser states are reproducible.

![Picture feedback version of Secret Number in Chrome after a low guess. A bug appears with the Too low! clue.](../figures/chapter_05/picture-too-low.png){#fig-ch05-picture-low fig-alt="The Secret Number page shows the guess 3, the text Too low!, and a colorful bug image." width="100%"}

![Picture feedback version of Secret Number in Chrome after the correct guess. A gem appears with the Correct! message.](../figures/chapter_05/picture-correct.png){#fig-ch05-picture-correct fig-alt="The Secret Number page shows the guess 6, the text Correct!, and a purple gem image." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** A wrong guess keeps the bug clue. A correct guess changes the same `<img>` element to `gem.svg` and updates its `alt` description. The text clue remains visible so players do not have to rely on the picture alone.

`feedback.src` means “which picture should the feedback image show?” The code changes that file name when the answer is correct. It also changes `feedback.alt`, so the spoken description matches the new picture. The player still uses words and numbers to understand the clue; the picture adds a quick visual reward.

:::

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | How comparisons really work" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Conditions are expressions that become `true` or `false`. Prefer `===` over `==` because `===` compares both value and type. `Number(input.value)` converts typed text into a number before comparison. You can combine conditions with `&&` (AND), `||` (OR), and ! (NOT).

```javascript
if (guess >= 1 && guess <= 10) {
  // valid range
}
```

**HTML constraints are not the whole game rule.** `type="number"`, `min`, and `max` describe an input and its validity constraints, but our custom click handler still needs to check the value. An empty string becomes `0` when passed to `Number()`.

For a stricter version, place this guard inside the handler before comparing with `secret`:

```javascript
const raw = guessBox.value.trim();
const guess = Number(raw);
if (raw === "" || !Number.isInteger(guess) ||
    guess < 1 || guess > 10) {
  message.textContent = "Enter a whole number from 1 to 10.";
  return;
}
```

Replace the original `const guess` line rather than declaring it twice. `return` exits this handler early.

Further reading: [MDN: number inputs and validation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/input/number).

:::

:::

::: {.callout-tip .challenge title="Challenge 2" icon="false"}

Add a rule: after 5 guesses, show the secret number.

# Create Reusable Game Actions {#sec-ch06}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 06 | Rock Paper Scissors]{.game-title}

[Parameters]{.skill-chip} [Return values]{.skill-chip} [Randomness]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .code-guide title="How to use the code pieces" icon="false"}

The short snippets below explain individual rules. The complete browser example later in this chapter combines them into a playable page.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- use function parameters and return values
- generate a random choice
- break a problem into small functions

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

As games grow, one giant function becomes difficult to understand. Small functions let us name behaviors such as `chooseComputerMove` and `decideWinner`.

:::

## A function can receive information

A parameter is a local name for information passed into a function.

![Functions can transform input into an output.](../figures/chapter_04/function-input-output.png){#fig-ch06 fig-alt="A simplified diagram sends a move into a function that compares rules and returns a result." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** A function receives information, performs work, and may return a result. This is a simplified picture: our actual `decideWinner(player, computer)` function needs **both** moves. The player choosing rock alone does not determine a winner.

```javascript
function cheer(playerName) {
  return "Go, " + playerName + "!";
}

const message = cheer("Ari");
```

## Make a random computer choice

`Math.random()` gives a value from 0 up to (but not including) 1. We can turn it into one of three choices.

```javascript
function computerChoice() {
  const choices = ["rock", "paper", "scissors"];
  const index = Math.floor(Math.random() * 3);
  return choices[index];
}
```

## Decide a winner

The rule function compares the player move with the computer move and returns a result.

```javascript
function decideWinner(player, computer) {
  if (player === computer) return "Tie!";

  if (
    (player === "rock" && computer === "scissors") ||
    (player === "paper" && computer === "rock") ||
    (player === "scissors" && computer === "paper")
  ) {
    return "You win!";
  }
  return "Computer wins!";
}
```

## Play the complete game in your browser {.unnumbered}

Save this page as `index.html`, or open `workspace/chapter6-rock-paper-scissors/index.html`. Each button passes a player move to `playRound()`, which asks `computerChoice()` for a move and displays the value returned by `decideWinner()`.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `index.html`]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Rock Paper Scissors</title>
  <style>
    body {
      margin: 0;
      min-height: 100vh;
      display: grid;
      place-items: center;
      background: #eaf4ff;
      color: #17243b;
      font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
    }
    main {
      width: min(90%, 480px);
      padding: 28px;
      border: 3px solid #17243b;
      border-radius: 20px;
      background: white;
      box-shadow: 8px 8px 0 #ffe48a;
    }
    h1 { margin-top: 0; color: #5d35d5; }
    .choices { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 10px; }
    button {
      padding: 12px 16px;
      border: 2px solid #17243b;
      border-radius: 12px;
      background: #f2edff;
      font: inherit;
      font-weight: 700;
      cursor: pointer;
    }
    button:hover, button:focus-visible { background: #dfd1ff; }
    #round, #result { min-height: 1.5em; }
    #result { font-size: 1.4rem; font-weight: 800; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>Rock Paper Scissors</h1>
    <p>Choose your move. The computer picks one too.</p>
    <div class="choices">
      <button type="button" data-move="rock">🪨 Rock</button>
      <button type="button" data-move="paper">📄 Paper</button>
      <button type="button" data-move="scissors">✂️ Scissors</button>
    </div>
    <p id="round" aria-live="polite">Pick a move to start.</p>
    <p id="result" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </main>
  <script>
    function computerChoice() {
      const choices = ["rock", "paper", "scissors"];
      const index = Math.floor(Math.random() * 3);
      return choices[index];
    }

    function decideWinner(player, computer) {
      if (player === computer) return "Tie!";

      if (
        (player === "rock" && computer === "scissors") ||
        (player === "paper" && computer === "rock") ||
        (player === "scissors" && computer === "paper")
      ) {
        return "You win!";
      }
      return "Computer wins!";
    }

    function playRound(player) {
      const computer = computerChoice();
      const result = decideWinner(player, computer);
      document.getElementById("round").textContent =
        "You chose " + player + ". Computer chose " + computer + ".";
      document.getElementById("result").textContent = result;
    }

    document.querySelectorAll("[data-move]").forEach(function (button) {
      button.addEventListener("click", function () {
        playRound(button.dataset.move);
      });
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

The demonstration pages set a known computer move and click Rock automatically for the next three screenshots. The playable page uses `Math.random()` each round.

![Rock Paper Scissors in Chrome before a move. Three buttons offer rock, paper, and scissors.](../figures/chapter_06/rps-start.png){#fig-ch06-rps-start fig-alt="A Rock Paper Scissors page has three move buttons and the prompt Pick a move to start." width="100%"}

![Rock Paper Scissors in Chrome when both moves are rock. The result is Tie!](../figures/chapter_06/rps-tie.png){#fig-ch06-rps-tie fig-alt="The page says You chose rock. Computer chose rock. and Tie!" width="100%"}

![Rock Paper Scissors in Chrome when rock beats scissors. The result is You win!](../figures/chapter_06/rps-win.png){#fig-ch06-rps-win fig-alt="The page says You chose rock. Computer chose scissors. and You win!" width="100%"}

![Rock Paper Scissors in Chrome when paper beats rock. The result is Computer wins!](../figures/chapter_06/rps-loss.png){#fig-ch06-rps-loss fig-alt="The page says You chose rock. Computer chose paper. and Computer wins!" width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** The computer choice is returned to `playRound()`, then both moves become arguments to `decideWinner()`. That function returns a result string. A tie returns immediately; otherwise the winning combinations are checked before the remaining result becomes “Computer wins!” The caller puts the returned text on the page.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | Parameters, return values, and local scope" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Parameters exist only inside the function call. A return value sends information back to the caller. This makes functions easier to test because the same function can work with different inputs and produce a result instead of depending on hidden global variables.

```javascript
function beats(a, b) {
  return (a === 'rock' && b === 'scissors');
}
const result = beats('rock', 'scissors');
```

**Argument or parameter?** In `beats("rock", "scissors")`, the strings are arguments: actual values supplied to the function. Inside the function, `a` and `b` are parameter names referring to those values during this call.

**Returning is not displaying.** `return` sends a value to the caller and ends this function call. The caller chooses whether to save it, display it, or use it in another decision.

The small `beats` example checks only rock against scissors. Use `decideWinner` for the complete three-move rules.

:::

# Make Things Change Over Time {#sec-ch07}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 07 | Catch the Star]{.game-title}

[Timers]{.skill-chip} [Coordinates]{.skill-chip} [CSS]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- use CSS position values from JavaScript
- use random coordinates
- use `setInterval` and `clearInterval`

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

A moving game world changes even when the player is not clicking. Timers let JavaScript run an action again and again.

:::

## Move an element

An absolutely positioned element can be moved by changing its left and top CSS properties.

![Game coordinates: x moves right, y moves down.](../figures/chapter_05/browser-coordinates.png){#fig-ch07 fig-alt="A coordinate plane starts at the top left. The x axis increases rightward and y increases downward; the star is at 25,35." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** Start at the top-left corner. Move 25 units right and 35 units down to reach the star. These are example coordinates, not fixed limits for your game; use the size of your own game area.

```javascript
star.style.left = "120px";
star.style.top = "80px";
```

## Pick a random position

A helper function makes the star jump to a new place.

```javascript
function moveStar() {
  const x = Math.floor(Math.random() * 280);
  const y = Math.floor(Math.random() * 180);
  star.style.left = x + "px";
  star.style.top = y + "px";
}
```

## Repeat an action with a timer

`setInterval` calls a function repeatedly. The number is milliseconds, so 1000 means one second.

```javascript
const timerId = setInterval(moveStar, 1000);

// Later, when the game ends:
clearInterval(timerId);
```

## Build the complete game

Put the pieces together. Type the code yourself if you can; typing helps your brain notice punctuation, spelling, and structure.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
<style>
  #game { position: relative; width: 340px; height: 240px; border: 2px solid #333; }
  #star { position: absolute; font-size: 36px; cursor: pointer; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Catch the Star</h1>
  <p id="score">Score: 0</p>
  <div id="game"><span id="star">⭐</span></div>
<script>
  let score = 0;
  const star = document.getElementById("star");
  const scoreText = document.getElementById("score");

  function moveStar() {
    const x = Math.floor(Math.random() * 280);
    const y = Math.floor(Math.random() * 180);
    star.style.left = x + "px";
    star.style.top = y + "px";
  }

  star.addEventListener("click", function () {
    score++;
    scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;
    moveStar();
  });

  moveStar();
  setInterval(moveStar, 1000);
</script>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `workspace/chapter7-catch-the-star/index.html` to watch the complete example. The star moves once per second, and a click raises the score and moves it immediately. The screenshot pages use known positions and control one timer callback so their states are reproducible.

![Catch the Star in Chrome at score zero, with the star near the upper left of the game area.](../figures/chapter_07/star-start.png){#fig-ch07-star-start fig-alt="The Catch the Star page shows Score: 0 and a yellow star near the upper-left corner of a bordered game area." width="100%"}

![Catch the Star in Chrome after one timer move. The star moves while the score stays zero.](../figures/chapter_07/star-after-timer.png){#fig-ch07-star-timer fig-alt="The same game shows Score: 0 with the yellow star near the middle-right of the game area." width="100%"}

![Catch the Star in Chrome after one click. The score is one and the star moves again.](../figures/chapter_07/star-after-click.png){#fig-ch07-star-click fig-alt="The game shows Score: 1 with the yellow star in a new position inside the game area." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** The timer calls `moveStar()` without a player action, changing `left` and `top` while the score remains zero. The click handler also calls `moveStar()`, but first it adds one to `score` and updates the paragraph. The regular page keeps its one-second timer; the demonstration pages control when the callback runs for the screenshots.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | CSS positioning and browser coordinates" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

For positioned HTML elements, left controls horizontal position and top controls vertical position. In browser coordinates, (0,0) is normally the top-left of the containing area, x increases to the right, and y increases downward. Element sizes matter when keeping an object inside the game area.

```javascript
star.style.left = x + 'px';
star.style.top = y + 'px';
```

**Which box do the coordinates belong to?** `#game { position: relative; }` makes the game area the containing block for the absolutely positioned star. Its offsets are measured from that area, not automatically from the entire page.

**Keep the whole object inside.** The largest useful x offset is approximately the game width minus the star width. The same idea applies to height.

**One timer is enough.** Keep the ID returned by `setInterval()` when you need to stop or replace it. Clearing a timer stops scheduled moves, not the separate click listener.

:::

# Draw Your Own Game World {#sec-ch08}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 08 | Bouncing Ball]{.game-title}

[Canvas]{.skill-chip} [Animation]{.skill-chip} [Velocity]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- create a canvas
- draw shapes with a 2D context
- animate with `requestAnimationFrame`

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

Canvas is different from ordinary HTML. Instead of moving page elements, your code redraws the game world frame after frame.

:::

## Meet canvas

The canvas element is a rectangular drawing surface. JavaScript asks it for a 2D drawing context.

![The animation/game loop repeats update and draw work.](../figures/chapter_06/animation-loop.png){#fig-ch08 fig-alt="A cycle connects read input, update state, draw, and next frame." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** Each frame is one trip around the cycle. Bouncing Ball has no keyboard input yet, so it begins by updating position. The next chapter adds player input before movement.

```javascript
const canvas = document.getElementById("game");
const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
```

## Draw a ball

A circle is an arc that goes all the way around.

```javascript
ctx.beginPath();
ctx.arc(x, y, 15, 0, Math.PI * 2);
ctx.fill();
```

## Animation is update + draw + repeat

Each frame changes the position, clears the old picture, draws the new picture, and asks the browser for another frame.

```javascript
function loop() {
  x = x + dx;
  y = y + dy;

  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
  drawBall();

  requestAnimationFrame(loop);
}
```

## Bounce at the edges

Reverse a velocity when the ball reaches a wall.

```javascript
if (x < radius || x > canvas.width - radius) {
  dx = -dx;
}
if (y < radius || y > canvas.height - radius) {
  dy = -dy;
}
```

## Build the complete game

Put the pieces together. Type the code yourself if you can; typing helps your brain notice punctuation, spelling, and structure.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Bouncing Ball</title>
  <style>
    body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; color: #17243b; }
    canvas { border: 2px solid #17243b; background: #f0f7ff; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Bouncing Ball</h1>
  <canvas id="game" width="500" height="300"></canvas>
  <script>
    const canvas = document.getElementById("game");
    const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
    let x = 100, y = 80;
    let dx = 3, dy = 2;
    const radius = 15;

    function drawBall() {
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.arc(x, y, radius, 0, Math.PI * 2);
      ctx.fillStyle = "#6d3df5";
      ctx.fill();
    }

    function loop() {
      x += dx;
      y += dy;
      if (x < radius || x > canvas.width - radius) dx = -dx;
      if (y < radius || y > canvas.height - radius) dy = -dy;
      ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      drawBall();
      requestAnimationFrame(loop);
    }
    loop();
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `workspace/chapter6-bouncing-ball/index.html` to watch the complete example. The browser redraws the purple ball on every animation frame. The screenshot pages pause automatic frames and call the same `loop()` function a known number of times.

![Bouncing Ball in Chrome near its starting position inside the canvas.](../figures/chapter_06/ball-start.png){#fig-ch08-ball-start fig-alt="A purple ball appears near the upper-left of a light blue bordered canvas." width="100%"}

![Bouncing Ball in Chrome after twenty more animation frames. The ball has moved right and down.](../figures/chapter_06/ball-after-frames.png){#fig-ch08-ball-frames fig-alt="The purple ball is farther right and lower in the same canvas." width="100%"}

![Bouncing Ball in Chrome after reaching the right wall and reversing horizontal direction.](../figures/chapter_06/ball-bounce.png){#fig-ch08-ball-bounce fig-alt="The purple ball is next to the right edge of the canvas." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** Every `loop()` call changes `x` and `y`, clears the previous drawing, and draws the ball again. At the right wall, `dx` becomes negative, so the next frames move left. The regular page uses `requestAnimationFrame()` to continue automatically.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | requestAnimationFrame and frame time" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

`requestAnimationFrame` asks the browser to run your animation code before the next repaint. Real games should not assume every computer draws the same number of frames per second. Advanced games use the timestamp passed to the callback to calculate delta time so motion depends on elapsed time, not frame count.

```javascript
let previousTime;
function loop(time) {
  const dt = previousTime === undefined
    ? 0
    : (time - previousTime) / 1000;
  previousTime = time;
  update(dt); // Speeds are in pixels per second.
  draw();
  requestAnimationFrame(loop);
}
requestAnimationFrame(loop);
```

**The timestamp is not the time since the last frame.** Subtract the previous timestamp and divide milliseconds by 1000 to get seconds. A speed of 180 pixels per second moves about 3 pixels in a 1/60-second frame.

This is a timing pattern, not a second loop to add beside the existing one. Supply your own `update(dt)` and `draw()` functions. Start the pattern with `requestAnimationFrame(loop)`. A more robust game should also handle a long pause, for example by resetting its previous timestamp when resuming.

Further reading: [MDN: requestAnimationFrame](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/requestAnimationFrame).

:::
